title: Morphological evolution of an Au crystalline domain in a nano-particle investigated by Bragg coherent diffraction imaging
authors: Seonghyun Han, Saehyun Kang, Ouyoung Kwon, Wonsuk Cha, Hyon Chol Kang, Chan Kim, Do Young Noh
abstract: Understanding the dynamic structural evolution of metallic nanoparticles is crucial for tailoring their functional properties. In this study, we utilized three-dimensional coherent X-ray diffraction to investigate the morphological transformation of Au nanocrystalline domains in a multi-domain nanoparticle during in-situ annealing. By combining Bragg coherent diffraction imaging with autocorrelation function analysis, we observed a transformation from an anisotropic multi-domain configuration toward a single crystalline equilibrium morphology. Above 600 degrees Celsius, a small subsidiary domain merged into the primary domain, which was continuously coarsened at 625 degrees Celsius, resulting in a more isotropic morphology. Finally, at 635 degrees Celsius, the low-energy {111} and {100} facets emerged, and the crystal shape converged toward an equilibrium truncated octahedral geometry. This work demonstrates a framework for interpreting complex domain dynamics, offering fundamental insights into domain growth and equilibrium shape formation.
summary: This work uses in-situ coherent X-ray diffraction to track how Au nanocrystalline domains reorganize during heating. By analyzing changes in diffraction patterns and domain correlation functions, the researchers observed the system evolving from a disordered, multi-domain state toward a stable, faceted truncated octahedron. This provides a fundamental framework for understanding domain growth and equilibrium shape formation in metallic nanoparticles.
main_problem: The study investigates the dynamic structural evolution of metallic nanoparticles, specifically tracking the transformation from an initial anisotropic multi-domain state to a single crystalline equilibrium morphology.
main_result: The Au nanocrystalline domains undergo continuous coarsening during annealing, eventually converging to a stable, faceted truncated octahedral geometry characterized by low-energy {111} and {100} facets.
method: The research employs in-situ three-dimensional coherent X-ray diffraction (BCDI) combined with autocorrelation function (ACF) analysis to non-destructively probe the structural changes during controlled thermal annealing.
model_or_system: The physical system is Au nanocrystalline domains embedded within a multi-domain nanoparticle, studied by monitoring diffraction patterns as a function of temperature up to 635 degrees Celsius.
key_observables: 3D diffraction patterns, line profile widths ($	ext{Q}_x-	ext{Q}_y$, $	ext{Q}_z$), autocorrelation function (ACF) shape, and the emergence of specific crystallographic facets ({111} and {100}).
important_parameters: Annealing temperature (e.g., $400^\circ	ext{C}$, $600^\circ	ext{C}$, $625^\circ	ext{C}$, $635^\circ	ext{C}$), X-ray energy (10 keV).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that BCDI and ACF provide a robust, artifact-free method for interpreting complex, time-dependent domain dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate temperature-dependent diffraction profiles showing peak merging and sharpening, and 3D renderings visualize the transition from anisotropic domains to the final truncated octahedral shape.
paper_structure: The paper follows a progression from initial characterization at low temperatures to observing domain merging at intermediate temperatures, culminating in the detailed analysis of facet formation and equilibrium shape convergence at the highest temperatures.
why_interesting: While focused on materials science, the study's rigorous use of time-resolved structural diagnostics (BCDI, ACF) to track non-equilibrium phase evolution and domain coarsening provides a powerful methodology applicable to understanding relaxation dynamics in complex quantum or many-body systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Bragg coherent diffraction imaging setup. A coher- ent X-ray beam, focused by a Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) mirror, illuminates an Au nanocrystal satisfying the Bragg condition. The diffraction signal is collected during an ω-scan to enable 3D image reconstruction of the nanocrystal.

FIG. 2. (a) 3D coherent diffraction profiles around the Au(111) Bragg peak at 400 ◦C, 600 ◦C, and 635 ◦C. The Qx–Qz and Qx–Qy cross-sections of the 3D diffraction pat- terns at each temperature are shown. At 635 ◦C, the fringe patterns corresponding to each plane become prominent. (b) Temperature-dependent line profiles along the in-plane direc- tion (Qx–y broad direction). The profile exhibits a double- peak structure at lower temperatures; however, as the tem- perature increases beyond 600 ◦C, it changes to a single-peak profile. (c) Temperature-dependent XRD profile widths in the Qz (blue) Qx–y broad (black),and Qx–y narrow (red) di- rections.

FIG. 4. Auto-correlation function (ACF) obtained from 3D coherent XRD. This is a slice plane corresponding to the Qx–Qy plane. The red dashed line indicates the boundary where the ACF drops to 1/e. The color scale was set to a maximum of 0.5. The domain morphology can be roughly identified from the ACF. Initially, it is elongated and gradu- ally thickens from 625 ◦C. At 625 ◦C, there is a dynamics that changes over time as atoms gradually attach and thicken.

FIG. 3. (a) Pearson correlation map calculated from 3D diffraction datasets acquired during in-situ annealing. The map illustrates the correlation of 3D XRD patterns as a func- tion of temperature change and experimental time within the same temperature range. The diagonal represents the self- correlation, which is equal to 1. (b) Line profile of the Pearson correlation coefficient along the red line shown in (a). Two major changes are observed at 600 ◦C and 625 ◦C. After the temperature is raised to 625 ◦C, the correlation coefficient changes continuously.

FIG. 5. (a) 3D rendering of BCDI images acquired at various annealing temperatures. For each temperature, the recon- struction was performed using a diffraction dataset acquired after the system reached a stabilized state. (b) Domain mor- phology resembling a truncated octahedron, observed at the final annealing stage of 635 ◦C. The crystalline facets are la- beled, and the phase values are displayed in both the top and side views of the domain.
